By Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press
LAS VEGAS – Let’s open with the “opener.”

Detroit Tigers manager Ron Gardenhire, who twice referred to himself as “old school” in his Wednesday morning press conference at the Winter Meetings, sounded open to the idea of using an “opener” pitcher to start games on occasion.

An “opener” has entered the present-day baseball vocabulary in recent seasons as a relief pitcher who starts a game for a short period of time, giving way to another relief pitcher. The strategy is implemented in large part to avoid having pitchers face opposing hitters more than two times in a game.

“I don’t have a problem with it,” Gardenhire said. “I saw the Twins do it to us, it seemed like every game. They got through it. Tampa Bay made it an art form. So if it’s part of the game, it’s part of the game.”
Gardenhire did not say the Tigers would implement such a strategy this season – the team currently has six starting pitchers – but it could be used on occasion when a starting pitcher hits the disabled list with an injury.
“It’s just something out there that everybody’s doing it, and I’m not afraid to try it if that’s the way it would have to be,” he said.

Though the starting rotation picture remains unclear, right-handers Jordan Zimmermann, Michael Fulmer and lefty Matt Boyd seem penned into the rotation. So, too, does righty Tyson Ross, who signed a one-year, $5.75 million deal on Monday. Barring injury, the final rotation spot could be a competition between lefties Daniel Norris and Matt Moore.
Both Ross and Moore spoke of the opportunity to start as reasons why they signed with the Tigers, but Gardenhire made clear that the team made no such guarantees.

“I don't think we've told anybody you're definitely this starter or that starter,” Gardenhire said. “We've told them all when we've signed them that you're going to get an opportunity to be a starter, and it's up to them on how they do in spring training and how they go about their business.”
Still, given the disparity in salary – Ross was paid nearly double than Moore – the team’s intentions are clear.
Gardenhire spoke on a number of other topics and provided some clarity to a couple of positional questions.
Entering his second season, Grayson Greiner is considered the Tigers’ starting catcher.
“Our thoughts are, Greiner’s going to be the guy,” Gardenhire said. “We think he can handle it. He did some pretty good things last year. It’s his turn.”
Greiner, 26, hit .219 in 96 at-bats, with no home runs and 12 RBI. He played in just 30 games.

John Hicks, who underwent groin surgery in August, will back up Greiner and also Miguel Cabrera at first base. The Tigers signed veteran Bobby Wilson to a minor league deal last month as major league-ready insurance.
And in the bullpen, righty Shane Greene is “absolutely” the team’s closer, Gardenhire said.
As much was assumed, but given Greene’s 5.12 ERA and 1.34 WHIP last season – along with the emergence of Joe Jimenez – Gardenhire’s confirmation was necessary.

“Unless they trade him,” he said. “Never know.”
Despite saving 32-of-38 games last season, Greene’s trade value has taken a hit. Entering his age 30 season, he has yet to display the consistency that teams covet when considering him for a trade, especially given his increasing salary.
In his second year of arbitration eligibility, Greene is projected to earn $4.8 million.
